title: Design: SAP reconciliation and agent evals
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic JEE-style quizzes for the backend and AI-engineering interview roadmap: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code writing, plus multi-correct questions. Language core, concurrency, DSA, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, LLM and agent engineering.
description: Designing a reconciliation pipeline between SAP and a data warehouse (idempotent loads, control totals, hash trees, break classification) and an eval and monitoring system for production LLM agents.
source: Kimball ETL practices; data engineering reconciliation write-ups; Merkle tree overviews; OpenAI and Anthropic eval guides; Hamel Husain and Eugene Yan evals writing; LangSmith/OpenTelemetry GenAI docs

questions.prompt: You design a nightly reconciliation between SAP and a data warehouse. Which property matters most for the load job?

options.text: It is idempotent and re-runnable per business date
options.why: Right: a failed or repeated run must not create duplicates or gaps.

options.text: It always runs as one huge transaction over all history
options.why: Huge transactions are slow, lock a lot and are hard to retry.

options.text: It deletes the warehouse tables first and reloads everything
options.why: Full reloads waste time and leave a window with no data.

options.text: It silently skips rows that fail to parse
options.why: Silent skipping creates exactly the discrepancies you are reconciling.

questions.explanation: Partition work by business date or document range, upsert by business key, and record the run id and counts.

questions.prompt: SAP reports 1,000,000 documents for the day. The warehouse holds 998,750 rows for it, of which 1,500 are duplicate loads of documents that are present (every warehouse document exists in SAP). How many distinct SAP documents are missing from the warehouse?
questions.explanation: Distinct documents in the warehouse = 998,750 - 1,500 = 997,250. Missing = 1,000,000 - 997,250 = 2,750. Equal counts can still hide problems, so also compare checksums.

questions.prompt: You compare hierarchical checksums (day, then half, then half again) to find the one mismatching partition among 1,024 partitions. How many comparison levels, halving each time, are needed to isolate it?
questions.explanation: log2(1024) = 10 halvings. Hash trees (Merkle trees) let you localise differences without comparing every row.

questions.prompt: Tables sap_invoices(doc_id, amount) and dwh_invoices(doc_id, amount) should match. Write one SQL query that lists doc_id values that are missing from dwh_invoices or have a different amount.

checks.label: joins or excepts the two tables

questions.model:
SELECT s.doc_id
FROM sap_invoices s
LEFT JOIN dwh_invoices d ON d.doc_id = s.doc_id
WHERE d.doc_id IS NULL OR d.amount <> s.amount;
questions.explanation: SELECT doc_id, amount FROM sap_invoices EXCEPT SELECT doc_id, amount FROM dwh_invoices is a shorter alternative. A FULL OUTER JOIN additionally finds rows that exist only in the warehouse.

questions.prompt: Match each typical reconciliation mismatch to the fix.

left.text: Records deleted or archived in the source

right.text: Reprocess a trailing window and use a watermark
Compare decimals with an agreed tolerance

questions.explanation: Classify breaks (missing, extra, changed, timing) in the report so owners can act on each class.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion and the reason, then choose the option that describes them correctly.
questions.assertion: The warehouse loader should upsert by the business key instead of blindly inserting.
questions.reason: After a failure the same batch is retried, and an upsert does not create duplicates.

whys.a: Right: idempotent writes make retries safe.

questions.explanation: Pair it with a unique constraint on the key so a bug cannot reintroduce duplicates.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion and the reason, then choose the option that describes them correctly.
questions.assertion: If row counts in SAP and the warehouse are equal, the data is proven to match.
questions.reason: Missing rows in one place can be offset by extra rows elsewhere.

whys.d: Right: the assertion is false, and the reason is true because offsets and changed values keep counts equal.

questions.explanation: Add sum-of-amount control totals and per-partition hashes to the count check.

questions.prompt: Write a Python function pass_rate(cases, agent) where each case is a dict with "input" and "expected"; it returns the fraction of cases for which agent(case["input"]) equals case["expected"].

checks.label: divides by the number of cases

questions.explanation: Real agent evals rarely use equality; use rubric graders, schema checks or an LLM judge, and run each case several times because outputs vary.

questions.prompt: Match each production-agent metric to what it tells you.

right.text: Whether the agent achieved the user's goal
Whether claims are supported by retrieved sources
How often tools fail or are called with bad arguments
Tokens and tool spend per completed task
How often safety rules are triggered
Disk usage of the vector store

questions.explanation: Track them per prompt/model version so a deploy can be compared against the previous baseline.

questions.prompt: An agent handles 50,000 runs per day. You sample 5% for an LLM judge that reads 4,000 tokens per judged run. How many millions of tokens does the judging consume per day?
questions.explanation: 5% of 50,000 = 2,500 runs; 2,500 x 4,000 = 10,000,000 tokens. Sampling keeps judging cost a small fraction of serving cost.

questions.prompt: An agent solves a task correctly 90% of the time and attempts are independent. What is the percent chance that three repeated attempts at the same task are all correct (one decimal place)?
questions.explanation: 0.9^3 = 0.729. Reliability metrics such as pass^k fall quickly with k, which is why consistency matters more than a single pass rate for agents.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion and the reason, then choose the option that describes them correctly.
questions.assertion: Run a fixed golden set of cases before every prompt or model change.

whys.a: Non-determinism is a reason to use thresholds, not the reason for a golden set.
whys.b: Right: both are true; the golden set exists to catch regressions, while non-determinism means you compare pass rates rather than exact outputs.

questions.explanation: Keep the set versioned, add every production failure as a new case, and gate deploys on score thresholds.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion and the reason, then choose the option that describes them correctly.
questions.assertion: Production monitoring should track drift in the input distribution as well as offline eval scores.
questions.reason: An offline eval set never becomes stale once it is written.

whys.c: Right: users change, so a fixed set drifts away from real traffic and must be refreshed.
whys.d: The assertion is the true statement.

questions.explanation: Sample production traces into the eval set regularly and compare topic and length distributions over time.

questions.prompt: Complete the monitoring plan for a production agent.
questions.text: Record {1} for every run, alert on a rising error {2} and on p95 latency, and send low-scoring samples to {3} review.
questions.explanation: A trace with every model call, tool call and token count lets you replay and debug any failed run.

questions.prompt: Which signals deserve an alert for a production agent? Select all that apply.

options.text: A jump in tool-call error rate after a deploy
options.why: Right: often a schema or dependency break.

options.text: Cost per task doubling over a day
options.why: Right: loops and retries burn tokens quietly.

options.text: A guardrail or PII-leak detector firing above its baseline
options.why: Right: safety signals need a fast response.

options.text: The average answer length changing by 1%
options.why: Small natural variation, not actionable on its own.

questions.explanation: Alert on user impact, safety and cost; keep fine-grained drift on dashboards.
